messages.subject: phylogram vs cladogram
parts:
There have been a few papers that have discussed the utility in using phylograms instead of chronograms in ancestral character state analyses. A recent article (and citations for other studies within) is here. 

Because many biogeographic questions are intrinsically tied to timing it is logical to use a dated phylogeny for BioGeoBEARS.

I do not have the correct sampling to accurately date my current phylogeny. I am therefore wondering if anyone has looked into the utility of running BioGeoBEARS with a phylogeny where branch lengths correspond to molecular evolution instead of time? 

The biggest issue I can think of is that logic of the linked paper does not necessarily extend into biogeography. That is, phenotypes are linked to molecular evolution hence the suitability of phylograms. But, biogeography may have a stronger link to time than to molecular evolution? 

Any thoughts on this are appreciated. I have an idea where the center of origin is for my species is, but it would be ideal to have an analysis to test this theory. 

Thanks!

messages.author: 967ac2c367fe0137
messages.subject: Re: phylogram vs cladogram
parts:
I was just reading this post http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#fix_short_trees and perhaps this advice from Dr. Matzke is the way to go, "If you have no good external dating information, but you want to estimate relative dates anyway (which is legitimate, if you state this clearly in your writeup), then in the BEAST setup, you should just put a tight normal prior on the date of the root, and give it a mean of, say, 1 or 10 or some such. Then you just recognize that all of your dates are relative to that prior constraint, and interpret your results accordingly." 

I just haven't seen that in other papers. Anyone have experience with this?

I've run a few rounds of biogeobears with an undated tree and although the results are as expected in terms of center of origin I get otherwise wonky results.
